notes:
I've put together notes for John 12:26–50. There are three gaps:

- **Missing pages.** I couldn't read past v. 25 of the full Enduring Word page, or past v. 13 of Calvin's commentary on StudyLight. For later verses I used short excerpts from Guzik's and Calvin's commentaries that turned up in searches.
- **No Orthodox, NET Bible or Bible Odyssey material.** None came up.
- **Nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching** for this passage.

Notes marked "page text" come from a page I read in full (Wesley's Notes, the Enduring Word chapter summary), not from a quotable search excerpt. The URL follows each point.

---

**v. 26**
- Wesley: following Jesus means "hating his life," as in v. 25. "Where I am" means heaven. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Guzik: the grain-of-wheat teaching in vv. 24–26 applies to Jesus' death and also to His disciples. They follow Him by losing their earthly life in order to keep it for eternal life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**v. 27**
- Guzik: the hour troubled Jesus because He knew what the agonies of the cross would involve. John doesn't describe Gethsemane, but the idea behind that prayer of Jesus is expressed in John 12:27-28. Quoting Morris, he reads "save Me from this hour" as a hypothetical prayer at which Jesus looks, but which He refuses to pray. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Jesus does not pull back from His Father's will. He first asks to be saved from the hour to show how tremendous a self-sacrifice that obedience involved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/john-12.html
- Wesley: the real question is not "what shall I choose?" His heart was already set on the Father's will; He was struggling for words. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Calvin draws a lesson. If Christ's sinless feelings needed restraining, we must work even harder against our sinful ones and persevere in doing violence to themselves, until they have denied themselves. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom35.ii.v.html
- Catholic (Augustine): His soul was troubled, not on His own account, but voluntarily for the sake of others. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701052.htm

**v. 28**
- Wesley: "I have glorified it" means through Jesus' entering this hour; "I will glorify it again" means through His passing through it. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary counts this as the third voice from heaven, after the baptism and the transfiguration, and this utterance is to a wider circle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-31.html
- Catholic (Augustine) gives two readings. One: I have both glorified it, before I created the world, and I will glorify it again, when He shall rise from the dead and ascend into heaven. The other: it was glorified through His birth, miracles and transfiguration. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701052.htm

**vv. 29–30**
- Wesley: the crowd heard a sound but not the words. Even great revelations can stay partly obscure "to exercise our faith." Thunder may really have come with the voice. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Calvin: John means only part of the crowd. He is pointing out that the greater part of men, while they hear God, do not hear him though he speak plainly and distinctly. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom35.ii.v.html
- The Homiletical Commentary on v. 30 says Jesus did not need an audible answer to His prayer (compare John 11:42). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-31.html

**v. 31**
- Guzik: The spirit of this world was judged by the way it treated Jesus at the cross. Satan was cast out of any rightful authority over God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Ligonier: here "world" means the fallen order opposed to God. His death is a judgment on the world because it marks the point at which He is decisively rejected by sinners. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/moment-judgment-and-salvation
- Constable: Jesus' death might appear to be a victory for Satan, but really it signaled his doom. His final destruction is still future (Revelation 20:10). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-31.html
- Vincent: In every case but one where the word ἐκβάλλω occurs in John, it is used of casting out from a holy place or society. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-31.htm
- Clarke (Methodist) has an unusual paraphrase. The world will judge and "cast out" Christ Himself: I, who am its ruler and prince, shall be cast out, shall be condemned by my own creatures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-31.html
- Catholic (Augustine): this is a present judgment, not the last one, that judgment by which the prince of this world shall be cast out. Satan is the prince of all the wicked who inhabit this world. He is driven out of believers' hearts. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701052.htm

**v. 32 — the main point where traditions differ**
- **Reformed and Calvinist Baptist:**
  - Ligonier: "all" means people from all kinds of backgrounds are drawn to Him, not each and every person. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/moment-judgment-and-salvation
  - Piper: the Greek has only "all" (*pantas*). Using John 11:52 as a parallel, it means not all human beings, but "all the children of God." https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-we-believe-about-the-five-points-of-calvinism
  - John Samson: "all" means Jews and Gentiles. If everyone were drawn in the John 6:44 sense, then all will be saved. https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/understanding-john-1232
  - Calvin: "all" must be understood to refer to the children of God, who belong to his flock. He agrees with Chrysostom that the word stresses Gentiles and Jews together. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom35.ii.v.html
  - Gill: the drawing is the efficacious grace of God to bring them, though without any force and compulsion, and is not true of every individual. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-32.html
- **Methodist and Arminian:**
  - Wesley: "Gentiles as well as Jews. And those who follow my drawings, Satan shall not be able to keep." He implies a person can choose whether to follow the drawing. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
  - Clarke: by the preaching of the word and the influence of the Spirit, Christ will attract and illuminate both Jews and Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-32.html
  - GotQuestions explains that Wesleyans use this verse for "prevenient grace": a grace won by Christ's cross that works in all people. The verse is frequently used to object to the Reformed position of irresistible grace. https://www.gotquestions.org/prevenient-grace.html
- **Anglican:** Archbishop Trench argues that anyone who denies irresistible grace must read "draw" as nothing more than the potent allurements, the allective force of love. https://biblehub.com/sermons/john/12-32.htm
- **Non-Calvinist Presbyterian (Barnes):** Christ will make the way open by the cross, so that all men may come. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-32.html
- **Calvinist Baptist preaching (Spurgeon):** If Christ Jesus is seriously preached he will draw all men to himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-32.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** he follows the Latin reading "all things," for all men have not faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701052.htm Calvin replies that the agreement of all the Greek manuscripts ought to have greater weight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/john-12.html

**v. 33**
- Guzik: Jesus knew not only that He would die but that He would be crucified. Jesus knew the painful and humiliating manner of His death, but still obeyed God's will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- GotQuestions: the main reference is the cross, but His words also include the resurrection and ascension in its meaning. https://www.gotquestions.org/if-I-be-lifted-up.html

**v. 34**
- Precept Austin: the crowd misread messianic prophecy. "Law" could mean the whole Old Testament. Of the passages mentioned, Ps 89:36–37 is the most likely candidate. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-12-commentary
- Wesley: there is no real conflict. "He first dies, and then abideth for ever." (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm

**vv. 35–36**
- Guzik: We must believe on Jesus while the light is there, because it won't last forever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Precept Austin: There is a finite, limited time in which each individual has opportunity to respond to the Light. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-12-commentary
- Coffman (Restoration Movement): Israel's day of grace was fading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/john-12.html
- Wesley: "the light" means Jesus and His teaching. "Children of light" are God's children, "wise, holy, happy." (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm

**vv. 37–38**
- Wesley: the "arm of the Lord" is God's power shown in Christ's preaching, miracles and redemption. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- A Bible Hub sermon outline (D. Thomas) says unbelief was Not for want of evidence. https://biblehub.com/sermons/john/12-39.htm

**vv. 39–40 — the second main point where traditions differ**
- **Reformed:**
  - Calvin admits that the plain sense is "harsh": the power of believing was taken from them. He answers that there is no absurdity in this, if nothing could happen different from what God had foreseen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-39.html
  - On v. 40, Calvin says God makes His word a punishment to the reprobate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-40.html
  - Gill (Baptist): God hardens not by any positive act, but by leaving and giving men up to the blindness and hardness of their hearts. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/john/12-40.html
- **Methodist:**
  - Wesley: they could not believe "by the just judgment of God, for their obstinacy and wilful resistance," they were at length so left to the hardness of their hearts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
  - Clarke: they could not believe the miracles because they had already rejected the prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-39.html
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** "could not" means real impossibility, but the impossibility came from earlier choices: Wilful rejection had been followed by rejection which was no longer within the power of the will. https://biblehub.com/john/12-39.htm
- **Lutheran (Bengel):** they first refused to believe and then could not. They are mistaken, who suppose what is said to be in the inverse order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-39.htm
- **Presbyterian (Barnes):** "could not" means only that faith cannot coexist with blindness while the blindness lasts. It determines nothing about their power of removing that blindness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-39.htm
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):** as with Pharaoh, God will confirm you in your position. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-40.html
- **Guzik:** God's judgment strengthens people in the choice they have already made. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- **Catholic (Augustine, in Aquinas's *Catena Aurea*):** if any ask why they could not believe, I answer, because they would not. God hardens by forsaking and not supporting him. The *Catena* also explains "could not" as meaning that the prophet could not be wrong, not that it was impossible that they should believe. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wyc/john/12-38.html
- **Modern scholarship (Meyer):** John cites Isaiah 6 freely. The one doing the blinding is neither Christ ... nor the devil ... but ... God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-39.htm

**v. 41**
- Wesley: the glory Isaiah saw (Isaiah 6) was Christ's, and Isaiah 6 calls it the glory of the LORD, "Jehovah, the Supreme God." (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: few New Testament statements more strikingly show the apostles' belief touching the pre-existence of the Lord and His identity with the God Isaiah saw. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-12.html

**vv. 42–43 — were these real believers?**
- Pulpit Commentary: John mentions these believers not to mitigate the charge. His point is that they lacked the courage to declare their faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-12.html
- Calvin: they were probably not completely silent, but the proper kind of profession was, openly to declare that they were the disciples of Christ. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom35/calcom35.ii.viii.html
- Clarke (Methodist): the only two we can name are Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea. They were as yet weak in the faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-42.html
- Steven Cole (bible.org) thinks they may have come to faith later, but Unless they later became willing to confess Christ whatever the cost, I contend that their faith was not saving faith. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-69-why-people-don-t-believe-jesus-john-1236b-43
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) takes the opposite line. He calls the verse opposed to the Lutheran heresy of justification by faith only. In his view what they lacked was not faith (they had it all) but obedience, meaning confession and baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-43.html
- Barclay: secret discipleship contradicts itself: "either the secrecy kills the discipleship, or the discipleship kills the secrecy." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-43.html

**vv. 44–45**
- Wesley: vv. 44–50 are John's epilogue to Jesus' public teaching, "a kind of recapitulation." "Seeth me" means seeing by the eye of faith. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: no one can believe Jesus' words without believing the Father, who sent as Messenger his own honored and beloved Son. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-12.html

**vv. 47–48**
- Wesley on v. 47: "Not now." He adds that Christ came to save even those who finally perish, since they too belong to the world He died for. This is an Arminian point. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the Word's main purpose is eternal life. Man turns it into judgment by rejection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-12.html
- Coffman: here the basis of the eternal judgment will be the word of Jesus Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/john-12.html

**vv. 49–50**
- Coffman: Jesus never requested men to believe him AS A MAN, but as the TRUE MESSENGER OF GOD. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/john-12.html
- There are two readings of "His command is eternal life":
  - W. Hall Harris (quoted on Precept Austin): Jesus does not say here that keeping the Father's commandment leads to eternal life, but that the commandment itself is eternal life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-12-commentary
  - Wesley: the command, when kept, is the way to eternal life and its beginning. (page text) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/12.htm
- Matthew Henry: "I know" shows how cheerfully and confidently Christ carried out His mission. It also intimates how justly those will perish who reject Christ and his word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_012.cfm
